steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the lead section of an encyclopedia article about the 2009 Sidekick data loss, when T-Mobile Sidekick users lost their data stored on Microsoft-run servers: what happened, why, the fallout and how the data was recovered.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What happened and who was affected
- Background: Danger, Microsoft acquisition
- Timeline of the outage
- Causes and blame
- Impact on cloud computing and Microsoft
- Class action lawsuit
- Recovery and Microsoft's response
- Existing backup application

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What happened
  - 2009 Sidekick outage; est. 800,000 US smartphone users temporarily lost personal data (emails, address books, photos)
  - servers run by Microsoft
  - phone: Danger Hiptop aka "Sidekick", on T-Mobile network
  - called biggest disaster in cloud computing history at the time
- Background
  - Sidekick originally made by Danger, Inc.; Microsoft bought it February 2007
  - ex-Danger staff absorbed into Mobile Communications Business (MCB), Entertainment and Devices Division; worked on Project Pink
  - most ex-Danger employees soon left Microsoft
  - Microsoft took over the data servers; its data centers hosted the data when lost
- Timeline
  - Friday, October 2, 2009: users notice data service outages
  - outages lasted about two weeks
  - October 10, 2009: T-Mobile announces data permanently lost (turned out incorrect)
- Causes / blame
  - Financial Times: Microsoft said data center acquired from Danger 18 months before not "updated to run on Microsoft technology"
  - company statement: "a confluence of errors from a server failure that hurt its main and backup databases supporting Sidekick users"
  - The Register: triggered by remedial work by contractor Hitachi Data Systems on Danger's Storage area network
  - T-Mobile blamed Microsoft
- Impact
  - public loss of confidence in cloud computing, already hit by outages and data losses in 2009
  - bad for Microsoft, then pitching cloud services to corporate clients (Azure, My Phone)
- Lawsuit
  - October 14, 2009: class action against Microsoft and T-Mobile
  - [quote: lawsuit allegation about failing basic data protection principles]
  - settled 2011: "$35 T-Mobile gift card, a $17.50 check payment, or up to 12 free downloadable items"
- Recovery
  - October 15: after 24x7 effort led by Glenn Beeswanger, Mark Hydar, Alan Levin, Microsoft recovered most or all data, would begin restoring
  - Steve Ballmer disputed data loss, called it an outage: "It is not clear there was data loss"; but "not good" for Microsoft
- Backup application
  - Danger already marketed a Windows app backing up Sidekick data to the user's computer, edits re-downloaded in real-time
  - users with it saved all their data
  - T-Mobile sold it in US for one-time $10
  - after restore, T-Mobile merged Sidekick storage website into regular T-Mobile backup site; PC app, Danger site and T-Mobile site could sync together

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Sidekick data outage of 2009 caused an estimated 800,000 smartphone users in the United States to temporarily lose personal data from their mobile handsets, such as emails, address books and photos. The data was held on computer servers that were run by Microsoft. The phones affected were the Danger Hiptop brand, which is also known as the "Sidekick", and they were connected through the T-Mobile cellular network. At the time it was described as the biggest disaster in the history of cloud computing.

The Sidekick smartphones were first produced by Danger, Inc., and Microsoft bought this company in February 2007. After the acquisition the former Danger staff were absorbed into the Mobile Communications Business (MCB) of the Entertainment and Devices Division at Microsoft, and there they worked on a future Microsoft mobile phone platform called Project Pink. But most of the ex-Danger employees left Microsoft soon to pursue other things. Microsoft took over running the data servers, and it was Microsoft's data centers that were hosting the customers' data when it was lost.

On Friday, October 2, 2009, users of T-Mobile Sidekick phones started to notice data service outages. These outages lasted for about two weeks. On October 10, 2009, T-Mobile announced that the personal information stored on Sidekick phones would be lost permanently, but this turned out to be incorrect.

The Financial Times reported that Microsoft said the data center it had acquired from Danger 18 months before had not been "updated to run on Microsoft technology." A statement from the company said the mishap was because of "a confluence of errors from a server failure that hurt its main and backup databases supporting Sidekick users." According to The Register, the precipitating event was remedial work done by the contractor Hitachi Data Systems on Danger's Storage area network. T-Mobile blamed Microsoft for losing the data.

- Impact
  - public loss of confidence in cloud computing, already plagued by outages and data losses in 2009
  - problem for Microsoft, trying to sell cloud services (Azure, My Phone) to corporate clients
- Lawsuit
  - October 14, 2009: class action against Microsoft and T-Mobile
  - quote of the allegation: "T-Mobile and Microsoft promised to safeguard the most important data their customers possess and then apparently failed to follow even the most basic data protection principles. What they did is unthinkable in this day and age."
  - settled 2011: "$35 T-Mobile gift card, a $17.50 check payment, or up to 12 free downloadable items."
- Recovery
  - October 15: 24x7 recovery effort (Glenn Beeswanger, Mark Hydar, Alan Levin); most or all data recovered, restore to begin
  - Ballmer: outage not data loss, “It is not clear there was data loss"; "not good" for Microsoft
- Backup app
  - Danger Windows app: back up Sidekick data to computer, changes re-downloaded in real-time
  - users with it saved all data; T-Mobile charged one-time $10 in US
  - afterwards Sidekick storage website folded into T-Mobile backup site; PC app, Danger site, T-Mobile site synced together

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The Sidekick data outage of 2009 caused an estimated 800,000 smartphone users in the United States to temporarily lose personal data from their mobile handsets, such as emails, address books and photos. The data was held on computer servers that were run by Microsoft. The phones affected were the Danger Hiptop brand, which is also known as the "Sidekick", and they were connected through the T-Mobile cellular network. At the time it was described as the biggest disaster in the history of cloud computing.

The Sidekick smartphones were first produced by Danger, Inc., and Microsoft bought this company in February 2007. After the acquisition the former Danger staff were absorbed into the Mobile Communications Business (MCB) of the Entertainment and Devices Division at Microsoft, and there they worked on a future Microsoft mobile phone platform called Project Pink. But most of the ex-Danger employees left Microsoft soon to pursue other things. Microsoft took over running the data servers, and it was Microsoft's data centers that were hosting the customers' data when it was lost.

On Friday, October 2, 2009, users of T-Mobile Sidekick phones started to notice data service outages. These outages lasted for about two weeks. On October 10, 2009, T-Mobile announced that the personal information stored on Sidekick phones would be lost permanently, but this turned out to be incorrect.

The Financial Times reported that Microsoft said the data center it had acquired from Danger 18 months before had not been "updated to run on Microsoft technology." A statement from the company said the mishap was because of "a confluence of errors from a server failure that hurt its main and backup databases supporting Sidekick users." According to The Register, the precipitating event was remedial work done by the contractor Hitachi Data Systems on Danger's Storage area network. T-Mobile blamed Microsoft for losing the data.

The incident made the public lose confidence in the concept of cloud computing, which had already been plagued by a series of outages and data losses in 2009. It was also a problem for Microsoft, because at the time Microsoft was trying to convince corporate clients to use its cloud computing services, like Azure and My Phone.

On October 14, 2009, a class action lawsuit was launched against Microsoft and T-Mobile. The lawsuit alleged:

T-Mobile and Microsoft promised to safeguard the most important data their customers possess and then apparently failed to follow even the most basic data protection principles. What they did is unthinkable in this day and age.

The class action lawsuit was settled in 2011, and affected users were compensated with a "$35 T-Mobile gift card, a $17.50 check payment, or up to 12 free downloadable items."

On October 15, after a 24x7 recovery effort that was led by Glenn Beeswanger, Mark Hydar and Alan Levin, Microsoft said that they had been able to recover most or all of the data and that they would begin to restore it.

Steve Ballmer, the CEO of Microsoft, disputed whether there had been any data loss at all, and described it instead as an outage. Ballmer said, “It is not clear there was data loss". He did say, though, that the incident was "not good" for Microsoft.

Even before the data loss, Danger had marketed an application for Windows computers that would back up all the Sidekick data onto a user's computer, and also allow changes to be made and then re-downloaded to the Sidekick in real-time. Users who had this backup storage option were able to save all their data. T-Mobile marketed this application in the United States for a one-time charge of $10. Right after the data was restored to all the users, T-Mobile incorporated the Sidekick storage website into the regular T-Mobile backup site. Then the application on the user's personal computer, the Danger backup site, and the T-Mobile backup site could all be synchronized together.
